summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs it in matters of justice and civil status. Trans visitors therefore enter a legal regime in which gender recognition, detention policy and the criminal-law rights framework are set in Paris, while the territorial institutions in Papeete regulate much of daily life.

Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document. Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments, so a trans woman holding a male marker is held with men; BuzzFeed News, reporting in January 2018, treated that outcome as a legal grey area rather than a settled rule. The CGLPL, the national preventive mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that France's Law 2016-1547 removed any requirement for medical transition or surgery when changing the gender recorded in civil status, yet that no norms were ever adopted governing how detainees should be housed in line with that change. Serious violations were documented across French detention, and the CGLPL's framework applies to French Polynesia's prisons. A trans visitor detained in the territory is consequently exposed to housing arrangements that national regulators have themselves found incompatible with France's own gender-recognition law.

The national criminal-law framework supplies the protection machinery that reaches the territory. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, sexual identity was added in July 2012, and on 18 November 2016 gender identity replaced it in article 225-1 of the Penal Code, with the Labour Code covering sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. The conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022.

Gender-diverse healthcare inside French Polynesia is limited by the small number of specialists practising locally. Some trans residents, including rae-rae, face rejection from their families and leave for mainland France to obtain specialised services the archipelago cannot provide. An effort to narrow that gap failed: under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone on mainland France's terms, and after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed. The distance between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the islands remains the most concrete material constraint on a trans person staying any length of time.

Partner recognition follows French law. Civil solidarity pacts date from 1999, same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, joint adoption has remained rare since, and assisted reproduction was extended to lesbian couples from September 2021.

The cultural setting is unusually well documented. The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. The territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023, bringing territorial government and church representatives together with the University of French Polynesia. Reporting from OutTraveler on 4 July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.
tangentialFactors:
National medical and political institutions have moved in a restrictive direction, which frames the environment a trans visitor enters even where the territory itself stays quiet. The Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an epidemic-like phenomenon and a primarily social problem. A March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a health scandal and youth transness a social contagion. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, with no National Assembly action recorded since 23 July 2024, while late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Travel-industry material presents the islands through an LGB lens rather than a trans one. Out Adventures offers Tahiti and Bora Bora across the 118 islands as a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture, and its assessment reports no trans-specific finding for French Polynesia. OutTraveler's July 2025 piece works the same terrain, describing acceptance as cultural texture rather than legal guarantee.

Attitudinal data from elsewhere in France's overseas possessions suggests France's capital is not the only reference point. A 2014 survey found only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France, and Mayotte, another overseas collectivity, reports frequent family rejection and discrimination. These figures concern sexual orientation rather than gender identity, and no territorial breakdown for French Polynesia exists in the sources.
localsOnly:
Changing the gender recorded in civil status no longer requires medical transition or surgery under France's Law 2016-1547, and residents of French Polynesia process that change through the French civil-status system rather than through a territorial procedure.

Everyday recognition policy sits with territorial and national institutions. Since March 2019 French higher education institutions are expected to use trans students' preferred names, enrolment forms use parent 1 and parent 2, and schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign.

Residents who need endocrine or surgical care beyond what the islands can supply travel to mainland France, and family rejection is a documented driver of that move, particularly for rae-rae. The social-security bill that would have reimbursed progesterone and testosterone in full on mainland terms failed in the Territorial Assembly, so hormonal treatment remains short of the mainland reimbursement level.

The conversion-therapy ban that took effect on 1 February 2022 applies nationally, and residents may invoke article 225-1 of the Penal Code, the Labour Code protections and the 2017 aggravating circumstance for transphobic crime through French courts with jurisdiction over the territory.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a trans-specific violent incident, prosecution or police case in French Polynesia itself. The 2019 attack figures and the 2020 report documenting a 36% rise are national French data with no territorial breakdown.

The CGLPL opinion establishes that France's housing norms for trans detainees are missing and that serious violations persist across French detention, but the sources do not document a monitoring visit, inspection finding or case arising inside French Polynesia's prisons specifically. The extension of the CGLPL's remit to the territory is asserted at framework level, not evidenced by a territory-specific report here.

Whether the Senate bill banning medical transition under 18 advanced after the National Assembly's inactivity from 23 July 2024 is unresolved in the sources. The March 2024 compensation bill for men prosecuted under the repealed 1960 indecent-exposure clause likewise awaits a Senate vote, though it concerns sexual orientation rather than gender identity.

BuzzFeed News's characterisation of detention practice as a legal grey area dates from January 2018 and reports on France; whether French Polynesian prison administration has since deviated from the document-marker rule is not sourced. Out Adventures, the other travel-industry source, offers no trans-specific finding for the territory.

The claim that the territory has no Pride movement rests on a single July 2025 travel feature, and the 2023 colloquium's outcomes for trans residents are not detailed in the inventory.
